name: AI Drafting of Regulatory Documents
title: AI Drafting of Regulatory Documents
answer: Teams use AI to draft parts of investigational new drug applications, investigator brochures and nonclinical summaries, documents with rigid formats. One study reported nonclinical summary drafting fell from about 100 hours to 3 to 4 hours per batch with no critical regulatory errors under its criteria.

reading.body:
AI can compress nonclinical summary drafting from about 100 hours to 3 to 4 hours per batch, with no critical regulatory errors under the study's criteria.

The pattern is narrow and worth stating precisely. The work being automated is format-bound: investigational new drug applications, investigator brochures, nonclinical summaries. These are documents where the structure is fixed and the content is assembled from prior results, which is the kind of task language models handle without needing judgment about what the science means.

The reported saving is large enough to matter for AI specifically because it is measured in batches, not documents. Regulatory writing is a throughput problem for the teams that produce it, and a hundredfold reduction in drafting time changes how many submissions a fixed headcount can support. The study's error finding is the load-bearing part. No critical regulatory errors under its criteria is a claim about one study's review standard, not a general guarantee.

What the data does not cover is the review time. The reported savings rarely include it, and a pilot on your own documents is the only way to measure error rates that apply to you. Nothing here speaks to compute, buildings, or power. This is a software capability sitting on top of existing infrastructure, and it should be read as one.

sections.body: Measure error rates on your own documents in a pilot before scaling; reported savings rarely include the review time.
